newsitem.title: CHINA: China official calls for consumption tax hikes.
newsitem.headline: China official calls for consumption tax hikes.

text.p: China should raise consumption taxes on imported cigarettes, wines and cars, and on gems and jewellery and other products, the official China Daily on Tuesday quoted a senior tax expert as saying.

The scope of consumption taxes should be widened to include gourmet food, clothing, electronic appliances, brand cosmetics and other goods, said Liu Zhuo, deputy director of the Institute of Tax Sciences at the State Administration of Taxation.
Consumption taxes introduced in 1994 were still too soft on imported tobacco and wines, China Daily quoted Liu as saying.
The consumption tax on imported sedan cars stood at only eight percent, while the levy on jewellery was just 10 percent, he said, but gave no details of the scale of possible tax rises.

Cars imported into China are subject to a raft of taxes that, taken together, can more than double the cost of the vehicle. Foreign alcohol and cigarette producers have also complained about high tax rates on their products.

Consumption taxes raised 55.3 billion yuan ($6.66 billion) in 1995, up 10.8 percent from the year before, but they still accounted for only a tiny fraction of total tax revenues and were hampered by collection problems, China Daily said.
The taxes are levied on goods considered non-essential or luxurious, including cosmetics, skincare and haircare products, tyres, cars, motorcycles, petrol, diesel and fireworks.
